problems.title: Determination of Capacitance
problems.statement:
## Background

It is known that capacitors play a significant role in the electrical circuits. There are several methods of measurements of the capacitance of a capacitor. In this experiment you are required to perform the experiment in order to determine the capacitance of an AC capacitor using a simple electrical circuitry.

In Fig. 1.1 (a), a capacitor of capacitance $C$ and a resistor of resistance $R$ are connected in series to the alternating voltage source of mains frequency. The electrical power which is dissipated at the resistor $R$ depends on the values of $\varepsilon_0$, $C$, $R$ and frequency of the mains $f$. Graphical analysis of this relationship can be used to determine $C$.

## Materials and apparatus

1. capacitor
2. three resistors of known values with ±5% errors ( $R_A = 680\,\Omega$, $R_B = 1500\,\Omega$ and $R_C = 3300\,\Omega$ ) as shown in figure 1.1 (b).
3. step-down isolation transformer for alternating voltage source of $f = 50\ \mathrm{Hz}$
4. digital voltmeter
5. electrical connectors
6. linear graph papers

**Warning**: **The digital multimeter in this experiment will be used for measuring the rms voltage ($\tilde{V}$) across $R$ only. Do not use it to measure in other modes.**

## Instructions

figures.caption: Fig. 1.1 (a): AC Circuit for determination of capacitance C
figures.alt: Series AC circuit: a source labelled εo sin ωt (circle with a sine symbol) on the left, a capacitor labelled C above it, and a variable resistor labelled R (resistor with an arrow) on the right side of the loop.

figures.caption: Fig. 1.1 (b): A schematic diagram of the equipment used
figures.alt: Schematic of the equipment: a transformer fed from 220 VAC, 50 Hz; its secondary is connected through a capacitor C at the top to terminal D, and the bottom wire ends at terminal E; three resistors labelled RC, RB, RA stand side by side on the right, each with terminals at both ends.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: Derive the expression for the average power dissipation $\overline{P}$ in resistor $R$ in terms of $\varepsilon_o$, $R$, $C$ and $\omega$.

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: Deduce the condition for which $\overline{P}$ is a maximum.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: Convert the dependence found in a) into a linear dependence of certain quantities $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

parts.label: d)
parts.statement: Measure the root mean square (effective) voltage $V$ across $R$ for each of all possible combinations of $R_A$, $R_B$ and $R_C$.

parts.label: e)
parts.statement: Plot $\overline{P}$ versus $R$ and from this graph compute the value of capacitance $C$.

parts.label: f)
parts.statement: From c), draw the graph of $\alpha$ versus $\beta$ and determine capacitance $C$.

parts.label: g)
parts.statement: Estimate the uncertainties in the values of $C$ obtained in e) and f).

answer.note: Official sample results: 1.9 µF from the maximum of P versus R (e), 1.95 µF from the 1/(RP) versus 1/R² graph and 1.99 µF from the alternative R² versus (R/V)² graph (f).

figures.alt: Graph of P (W) versus R (Ω): 17 measured points joined by a curve rising from about 0.094 W at 410 Ω to a maximum of about 0.20 W near 1600 Ω and falling to about 0.11 W at 5480 Ω; dotted lines mark the maximum at 0.20 W and R ≈ 1600 Ω. Axes: P from 0.00 to 0.25, R from 0 to 6000.
Linear graph of 1/(RP̄) in (ΩW)^-1 versus 1/R² in (×10^-6 Ω^-2): points on a straight fitted line labelled y = 0.004x + 0.0015; vertical axis 0.000 to 0.030, horizontal axis 0.00 to 7.00.

Linear graph of R² (×10^6 Ω²) versus (R/V)² (Ω/V)²: points on a straight fitted line labelled y = 6.4428 x - 2.5428, crossing the vertical axis below zero; vertical axis -5.00 to 35.00, horizontal axis -1.000 to 6.000.
